 Why Costa Ricans Head for Puriscal When the Rains Stop
 By Guest Author 
 November 18, 2026 
 Share 
 Facebook X WhatsApp Email 
 Garrett Britton 
 Ask a Costa Rican where to go on a Sunday in late November and there is a good chance the answer will be Puriscal. The city sits in the hills about an hour west of San José, close enough for a day trip and far enough to feel like the countryside most Ticos remember from childhood. For a few weeks between the end of the rains and Christmas, everything that makes the place worth the drive arrives at once.
 Puriscal has never needed a beach or a volcano to draw visitors. What it offers is simpler: winding ridge roads, long views across the Central Valley, small farms, butcher shops with wood fires going and a pace of life that the capital lost long ago . This is the season when all of that is at its best.
 The first reason is the weather. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) forecast the dry season to settle over the Central Valley during the second week of November, and in Puriscal the change is easy to feel. Afternoon downpours give way to blue skies, and the trade winds that Costa Ricans call the Christmas winds begin to blow across the ridges.
 Those winds matter here more than in most places. They clear the haze, cool the air and open up views that stay hidden behind cloud for much of the rainy season. On a clear December morning a visitor can stand on a ridge above Santiago de Puriscal and see the valley on one side and the hills falling away toward the Pacific on the other.
 The timing also flatters the land. The rainy season has left the hills green, though in a drier-than-normal El Niño year the pastures may start turning gold sooner than usual. Back roads that turn to mud in the wet months are dry and passable again, which opens routes through villages that many visitors never reach.
 The second reason is pork. Puriscal is known across the country as the home of the chicharrón, and families here have been raising pigs and curing meat for generations. People drive out from San José every weekend of the year for a plate of fried pork with yuca, tortillas and a squeeze of lime, but in the weeks before Christmas the habit becomes a pilgrimage.
 The reason is the Feria del Chicharrón , the fair that has filled the center of Santiago de Puriscal in the early weeks of December for more than two decades. Vendors start frying before the morning mist has lifted, and by midday the smell of pork and woodsmoke has spread across the town. Past editions have added live music, craft stalls, carnival rides and a horse parade to the food.
 The crowds are real and the fair has drawn more than 6,000 visitors to the canton in a single week, a large number for a town of this size. Last year it opened on the last weekend of November and ran through Dec. 8, and anyone planning a trip this year should check the dates with the organizers before setting out.
 The calendar does the rest since the aguinaldo, the extra month of salary that Costa Rican workers receive at the end of the year, lands in December, and the school year ends around the same time. Families have a little more money and a lot more free time, and a drive to Puriscal costs far less than a weekend at the coast.
 Pork is also the meat of the Costa Rican Christmas. It goes into the tamales that families make together in December and onto the table as roast leg on Christmas Eve. Plenty of visitors leave Puriscal with a cooler in the trunk, stocked by the same butchers their parents bought from.
 There is more to do than eat. The canton lies where the dry forest of the Pacific slope meets the wetter forest of the highlands, and that mix draws birdwatchers, who find the trails easier going once the rains stop. Others come for the old tobacco country, the roadside stands selling fruit and local produce or simply the drive itself.
 What Puriscal offers in these weeks is a version of Costa Rica that many people assume has disappeared. It has clean air, green hills, good food cooked over a fire and neighbors who still greet strangers in the street. Costa Ricans have always known where to find it, and this is the time of year they go.
